    Temporal statistics of MSSR maps

    Source: vignettes/temporal.Rmd
    temporal.Rmd

    Temporal MSSR (t-MSSR) computes the single-frame MSSR map of every frame of a sequence and then reduces the stack of maps pixel by pixel with one temporal function (Torres-Garcia et al. 2022, Fig. 7a and Supplementary Note 5.2). mssr_temporal() does this with the definitions of Supplementary Table S2. Everything here is synthetic and generated in this document.

    A synthetic sequence

    Three emitters blink independently: two close to each other and one apart. Each frame adds Poisson noise to the blurred emitters on a faint background.

    set.seed(7)
size <- 20
g <- expand.grid(r = seq_len(size), c = seq_len(size))
spot <- function(r0, c0) exp(-((g$r - r0)^2 + (g$c - c0)^2) / (2 * (3 / 2.3548)^2))
emitters <- cbind(spot(10, 7), spot(10, 10), spot(5, 15))
frames <- array(0, c(size, size, 60))
for (t in seq_len(60)) {
  on <- stats::runif(3) < 0.4
  frames[, , t] <- stats::rpois(size^2, 25 * (emitters %*% on) + 2)
}
dim(frames)
#> [1] 20 20 60

    mssr_stack() stores the per-frame maps, so the statistics below need MSSR only once per frame. Every per-frame setting means what it means in mssr().

    s <- mssr_stack(frames, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
s
#> <mssr_stack> 60 frames of 40 x 40 MSSR maps (amp 2, order 1, fwhm 3 px)
#>   frames 1 to 60 of the input; 0 degenerate; engine mssr_r_rev3
#>   Use mssr_temporal() for a temporal statistic of the maps.
m <- mssr_temporal(s, "mean")
v <- mssr_temporal(s, "var")
k2 <- mssr_temporal(s, "sofi2")
v
#> <mssr_result> temporal_var
#>   input 20 x 20 -> output 40 x 40 (amp 2, extent grid)
#>   var of 60 frame(s) (frames 1 to 60)
#>   per frame: fwhm 3 px, order 1, kernel disk (half-size 3), mesh TRUE
#>   0 degenerate frame(s), 0 frame(s) with warnings; path stack
#>   trend (last / first tenth of frames) 1.03; mesh index 0.0725 (below_median, 194 pixels)
#>   Temporal statistic of nonlinear structure maps, not a quantitative intensity.
    op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
show(apply(frames, c(1, 2), mean), "mean of raw frames")
show(as.matrix(m), "mean of maps")
show(as.matrix(v), "variance of maps")
show(as.matrix(k2), "SOFI2 of maps (signed)")

    graphics::par(op)

    The panels show what each statistic does to these particular frames; they do not show that any statistic resolves the emitters better.

    Definitions

    Per pixel, x_1, ..., x_M are the maps’ values, m their mean and d_t = x_t - m.

    statistic Value Minimum frames
    "mean" m 1
    "var" (1/M) sum(d_t^2), the population variance 2
    "tpm" (sum(x_t))^2 = M^2 * m^2 1
    "cv" var / m, the supplement’s “CV” (0 where m = 0) 2
    "sofi2" mean of d_t d_{t+1} 2
    "sofi3" mean of d_t d_{t+1} d_{t+2} 3
    "sofi4" fourth-order lagged cumulant 4

    TPM shows nothing the mean does not, for non-negative maps:

    all.equal(mssr_temporal(s, "tpm")$values, 60^2 * m$values^2)
#> [1] TRUE

    The SOFI statistics use signed deviations at consecutive lags, so noise that is independent between frames does not enter their expectation. Orders 3 and 4 change sign with the emitters’ duty cycle; sign = "absolute" returns the absolute value for display.

    k4 <- mssr_temporal(s, "sofi4", sign = "absolute")
range(k4$values)
#> [1] 4.568025e-08 2.661497e+03

    "cv" is literally Var / Mean, an index of dispersion rather than the standard deviation divided by the mean, and it takes the sign of the mean.

    Reading the outputs

    The outputs are temporal statistics of nonlinear structure maps. They are not quantitative intensities, and no resolution gain is implied:

    • Variance, "cv" and SOFI of per-frame MSSR maps, and higher MSSR orders, can show two maxima where there is a single emitter.
    • When emitters are rarely on and dim, MSSR of nearly empty frames adds maxima to every statistic.
    • "var", "cv" and SOFI also respond to bleaching and drift (see trend below). Correct them first, and record what was done.
    • With amp > 1, signal-free regions show a sub-pixel grid of period amp. The article recommends Fourier interpolation for temporal analysis; the package amplifies with the supplement’s cubic kernel and mesh compensation instead.

    diagnostics$mesh_index measures the grid as the range of the mean over the amp x amp sub-pixel phases, relative to the mean. Where structure is present the index would mix structure and grid, so it uses only signal-free input pixels: by default those whose raw temporal mean is strictly below its median, or a background mask you supply. For the SOFI statistics it is computed on the absolute values, since signed cumulants average to about zero off the structure. It is formed only on the default field-of-view-preserving grid, where each input pixel holds every phase once. A frame subset of an mssr_stack uses the stack’s raw mean over all its frames, recorded as mesh_region = "below_median_stack".

    c(m$diagnostics$mesh_region, format(m$diagnostics$mesh_index, digits = 3))
#> [1] "below_median" "0.0286"
corner <- matrix(FALSE, size, size)
corner[16:20, 1:5] <- TRUE   # at least six pixels from every emitter
mssr_temporal(s, "mean", background = corner)$diagnostics$mesh_index
#> [1] 0.2578783

    diagnostics$trend compares the raw intensity in the last tenth of the frames with that in the first tenth. A large trend, from bleaching, drift or focus changes, inflates "var", "cv" and SOFI, which treat it as fluctuation; the package reports it and corrects nothing.

    v$diagnostics$trend
#> [1] 1.033109

    Relation to the authors’ tools

    The authors’ Python and MATLAB “SOFI” functions use absolute deviations at zero lag, and the Fiji plugin uses absolute deviations with lags that wrap around the ends of the acquisition. These are other statistics, so their outputs do not match mssr_temporal() by design. The authors’ R, MATLAB and Fiji variance divides by M - 1. vignette("method-concordance") lists the sources and every difference.

    Memory and time

    Statistics other than the mean and TPM need the mean before the deviations, so they pass over the frames twice. The per-frame maps are kept for the second pass when they fit the memory budget, and recomputed otherwise; both paths give the same values. mssr_estimate_resources() reports both estimates.

    est <- mssr_estimate_resources(c(512, 512), fwhm = 3, amp = 2, frames = 300,
                               statistic = "var")
est[c("stack_bytes", "stored_peak_bytes", "recompute_peak_bytes")]
#> $stack_bytes
#> [1] 2516582400
#> 
#> $stored_peak_bytes
#> [1] 5435877120
#> 
#> $recompute_peak_bytes
#> [1] 402712320
